lesson.title: You Can't Fix Both for Free: The Type I and Type II Error Tradeoff
lesson.summary: For a fixed sample size, making a test stricter to reduce Type I error automatically raises the risk of Type II error, and the only way to lower both at once is to collect more data.
lesson.body:
Here is the tradeoff stated plainly, tying together the last two chapters. Lowering alpha, meaning demanding a smaller p-value before rejecting H0, directly shrinks the Type I error rate, since the probability of a Type I error equals alpha exactly. But shrinking the rejection region, by pushing the critical value further into the tail, simultaneously makes it harder to reject H0 even when H0 is genuinely false, which raises beta, the Type II error rate. Raising alpha does the reverse, more false alarms but fewer missed detections. For a fixed sample size, alpha alone cannot shrink both error rates at once, this is a real, mathematical tradeoff, not just a cautionary saying.

A numeric illustration makes this concrete, using the critical values from the significance level chapter. For a two-sided z test, alpha = 0.05 sets critical values at z = plus or minus 1.96, while alpha = 0.01 pushes them out to about z = plus or minus 2.576. Suppose a real effect in some situation would reliably produce a test statistic around z = 2.30, a genuine, moderate departure from H0. At alpha = 0.05, the absolute value of 2.30 is greater than 1.96, so this result falls in the rejection region and correctly rejects the false H0. But at alpha = 0.01, the absolute value of 2.30 is less than 2.576, so this same result lands inside the fail-to-reject zone, a Type II error, a real effect that the stricter test missed entirely. Tightening alpha from 0.05 to 0.01 did not just reduce false alarms, it also made this particular true effect harder to detect.

There is a way out of the tradeoff that does not require touching alpha at all: increasing the sample size n shrinks the standard error, since standard error involves dividing by the square root of n, which sharpens the sampling distribution around the true parameter value. A sharper distribution means real effects produce more extreme test statistics without needing to loosen alpha, so a larger sample can lower Type II error without raising Type I error at all. This is why researchers who need both a strict alpha and a low chance of missing real effects invest in larger samples, rather than simply nudging alpha back and forth.

Every hypothesis test is a balancing act between two kinds of mistakes that can never be fully eliminated, only managed: falsely rejecting a true H0, a Type I error, and failing to reject a false H0, a Type II error. The significance level alpha is the dial set in advance for the first kind of risk, sample size and study design are the main levers for controlling the second, and a well-designed study picks both deliberately, based on what each kind of mistake would actually cost, rather than by default habit.
